proposal: Make a command-line tool that prints the lines, words and characters of standard input (Python 3.9, standard library only) count words and characters by the definitions in its specification: words are runs of letters, digits, apostrophes and hyphens, and characters are Unicode code points. The first prototype, at version 0.0, splits words at white space and counts bytes. Its function count(text) returns (lines, words, characters). Each of 18 use cases is a run of the tool graded 0 to 1 against the specification.
feedback: The design fits the specification's definitions of words and characters, and the numbers hold: the run grades (one score per use case, 0 to 1) total 12.9 of 18, and the six use cases the proposal names add at least 4.8. Two changes. First, drop the proposed edit to the specification. The specification already defines both counts; the prototype departs from them, which is a limit of the build, and a fix to a build's limit needs no edit to the specification (the project's review rules). 'Every other character separates words' already follows from the definition of a word. Whether a combining mark belongs to the word it follows is a choice the specification leaves open, so per the project's standards it goes as one line in the project's record of choices the specification leaves open, not into the specification. Second, the check's last test does not decide the change: count("well-known, isn't it?")[1] == 3 already passes on 0.0, since str.split gives 'well-known,', "isn't", 'it?'. The other five tests fail on 0.0 and decide it. The proposal's author took all three corrections; approve stands.

pattern.context: A proposal fixes a build that departs from definitions its specification already states, and proves the fix with tests that should fail before the change and pass after it.
pattern.problem: The proposal edits the specification to restate what its definitions already imply and to settle a choice the specification leaves open. Its check also counts a test that already passes on the old version, so that test cannot show the fix worked.
pattern.solution: Make no edit to the specification for a fix to a build's limit. Record the open choice as one line in the project's record of open choices. Run each test of the check on the old version; keep as deciding only those that fail there, and label the rest as guards that pass on both.
pattern.consequences: The specification stays as written: 0 sentences added instead of 2, plus one line in the record of open choices. The check rests on the five tests that fail on the old version, so passing it shows the change itself fixed the counts.
